q: A county-run community college disciplines a student for handing out leaflets that criticize the college president. That same week, a privately owned shopping mall with no government ties ejects a different student who is handing out the same leaflet. Both students sue under the First Amendment. The college argues that the Amendment says “Congress shall make no law” and so doesn’t reach a county institution. How should the court rule?
o: Only the claim against the college, since the Fourteenth Amendment binds local governments but not private owners.
Both claims go forward, because a mall that opens itself to the public takes on the role of a public sidewalk and must respect leafleters.
Neither claim goes forward, because the text limits only Congress, and no later amendment changed whom the First Amendment binds.
Only the claim against the mall goes forward, because leafleting is press activity, which the Constitution protects even from private interference.
e: Rule: The Fourteenth Amendment incorporates the First Amendment against state and local governments. Private actors aren’t bound. The press has the same rights as everyone else.
oe: Correct. Although the text names Congress, the Fourteenth Amendment incorporates the First Amendment against state and local governments (Cantwell did so for Free Exercise). The First Amendment binds only the government, so a purely private mall isn’t bound, though private institutions may adopt speech policies voluntarily.
Opening property to the public doesn’t turn a private owner into the government. The First Amendment restrains state action, and the mall has no government ties.
The Fourteenth Amendment incorporates the First Amendment against state and local governments. A county college is a government actor.
The press clause gives the press the same rights as everyone else, not more, and neither speech nor press rights run against private actors.
topic: Foundations and compelled expression — Incorporation · state action

q: A school district adopts a mandatory read-aloud unit for kindergarten and first grade made up of picture books that present a child’s gender transition as something to celebrate. District guidance tells teachers to answer a child who objects on religious grounds by explaining that the objection is “unkind.” The district lets parents opt their children out of its Halloween activities and its family-life unit, but it refuses opt-outs from the read-aloud unit, citing the burden of tracking absences. Orthodox Jewish parents sue for an opt-out. What is the parents’ strongest argument?
o: The unit substantially interferes with their children’s religious upbringing, which triggers strict scrutiny even under a neutral policy, and the district’s other opt-outs undercut its claim of infeasibility.
The unit compels their children to affirm a belief they reject, and Barnette forbids requiring students to hear views their families oppose.
The unit is hostile to religion within the meaning of Masterpiece Cakeshop, because it conflicts with the families’ faith.
The parents need not show any burden, because their control over their children’s education continues in full inside a public school.
e: Rule: Mahmoud: a policy that substantially interferes with a child’s religious development (a Yoder-type burden) triggers strict scrutiny even if neutral. Other opt-outs and self-made administrative burdens undercut the government’s interest.
oe: Correct. Under Mahmoud, a Yoder-type burden triggers strict scrutiny even if the policy is neutral and generally applicable. The books are normative, they are taught by trusted teachers to very young children, and dissent is corrected. The district’s existing opt-outs undercut its claim that opt-outs are unworkable, and administrative problems of its own design don’t count.

Nothing in the unit requires a child to declare a belief, and Barnette didn’t treat exposure as compulsion. Mahmoud protects the parents by another route: a substantial burden on religious upbringing.
Masterpiece involved officials’ expressed hostility and the disparate treatment of comparable objectors. A curriculum’s conflict with a family’s beliefs isn’t hostility in itself.

Overstated. Mahmoud’s inquiry is fact-intensive: the specific beliefs, the nature of the curriculum, the children’s age, and the context. The parents must show a substantial interference, and the district then gets a chance to satisfy strict scrutiny.
topic: School coercion (Kennedy, Mahmoud) — Mahmoud v. Taylor · parental opt-outs

q: Months after a small congregation begins holding nighttime drumming ceremonies, central to its worship, in a rented warehouse, the town bans “percussive sound audible from a public way after 9 p.m.” The ordinance exempts high-school sporting events, concerts in the town park, fireworks, and “establishments licensed to serve alcohol.” Neighbors testify that the drumming is no louder than the bars down the street. The town argues that the congregation’s belief that drumming summons ancestral spirits is irrational. How should the court analyze the congregation’s Free Exercise claim?
o: The exemptions for comparable secular noise mean the ordinance isn’t generally applicable, so strict scrutiny applies, and it likely fails.
The ordinance is valid under Smith, because a noise rule is a classic neutral law that only incidentally burdens religion.
The claim fails at the threshold, because a court need not protect a belief that it finds illogical, inconsistent, or unsupported by any evidence.
The ordinance survives intermediate scrutiny as a time, place, and manner rule, because it doesn’t mention religion.
e: Rule: Lukumi: exemptions that leave comparable secular conduct untouched make a law not neutral or generally applicable, so strict scrutiny applies. Beliefs need not be logical to be protected.
oe: Correct. As with Hialeah’s animal-killing ordinances in Lukumi, the exemptions gerrymander the law so that it falls almost entirely on religious conduct. Underinclusiveness shows the law isn’t generally applicable and also defeats narrow tailoring. Whether the belief seems rational is irrelevant.
Smith covers only laws that really are neutral and generally applicable. Exempting bars, concerts, and fireworks while catching the congregation shows this one isn’t.
Religious beliefs need not be acceptable, logical, consistent, or comprehensible to others to merit protection (Lukumi). The question is sincerity, not reasonableness.
Facial neutrality isn’t enough; Lukumi looks at how the exemptions operate. And once a law burdening religion fails general applicability, the test is strict scrutiny.
topic: Free Exercise — Lukumi · gerrymandered exemptions

q: A county contracts with private nonprofits to run emergency shelters. Every contract requires the provider to accept all clients the county refers, “unless an exception is granted by the Director of Human Services in her sole discretion.” The Director has never granted an exception. A religious shelter, citing its faith, declines to house unmarried couples together in family rooms, and the county ends its contract. The county argues that its requirement is generally applicable because no exception has ever been granted. Which response is strongest?
o: The unused exception power itself defeats general applicability, so the county must justify denying this shelter an exception.
The requirement is generally applicable, but the shelter wins anyway because Fulton overruled Smith.
The requirement is valid, because the county has in fact treated every provider identically.
The shelter must prove that the Director granted exceptions to secular providers, because only actual favoritism shows a lack of general applicability.
e: Rule: Fulton: a system of discretionary, individualized exemptions makes a policy not generally applicable, even if unused. Strict scrutiny asks whether the government has a compelling interest in denying an exemption to this claimant.
oe: Correct. Fulton held that a formal system of discretionary, individualized exemptions makes a policy not generally applicable even if no exemption has been granted, because it invites officials to decide which reasons are worthy. Strict scrutiny then asks whether the county has a compelling interest in refusing an exemption to this claimant.
Fulton expressly declined to overrule Smith. The shelter wins because the exemption system takes the case outside Smith.
Identical treatment so far doesn’t help. What matters is the Director’s “sole discretion” to grant exceptions, whether or not she has used it.
Fulton required no actual favoritism. The existence of a discretionary exemption system is enough to trigger strict scrutiny.
topic: Free Exercise — Fulton · discretionary exemptions

q: A state pays tuition for high-school juniors and seniors to take courses at any accredited private college in the state, except colleges “that are religiously affiliated or that use program funds for religious instruction.” A student wants to take calculus and theology at an accredited Catholic college. The state offers two defenses: it wants a stricter separation of church and state than the federal Constitution demands, and paying for the courses would violate the Establishment Clause. Which is the best assessment?
o: Neither works: aid that flows through the student’s choice doesn’t establish religion, and stricter separation isn’t a compelling interest.
The state wins on its second defense, because using public money for theology courses directly establishes religion.
The state wins on its first defense, because “play in the joints” lets a state decline to fund religion even where funding would be lawful.
The exclusion is valid for the theology course but not for calculus, because Carson protects a school’s religious status but not religious use of funds.
e: Rule: Carson: a state that subsidizes private education can’t exclude religious schools because of their religious status or use. A stricter-separation interest isn’t compelling, but the state may end the program.
oe: Correct. Under Carson, once a state subsidizes private education it can’t exclude schools because they are religious, even when the money pays for religious instruction. Under Zelman, aid that reaches religious schools through genuine private choice is permissible. Wrinkle 2 lets government disfavor religion only when necessary to avoid an Establishment Clause violation, not to separate church and state more strictly than the Constitution requires. The state remains free to end the program or to keep its own public schools secular.
The money reaches the college only through the student’s independent choice, which Zelman and Carson treat as permissible.
That sense of play in the joints is in retreat: Trinity Lutheran, Espinoza, and Carson rejected it. An interest in stricter separation than the Constitution requires isn’t compelling.
Carson extended the rule from status to use. Maine excluded schools because they would use the money for religious instruction, and the Court struck down that exclusion too.
topic: Establishment, funding, and RFRA — Carson v. Makin · religious use

q: A city denies a mosque’s application to expand its prayer hall under a neutral zoning rule that limits building size in residential areas. The mosque sues under the federal Religious Freedom Restoration Act, arguing that the denial substantially burdens its religious exercise. What is the city’s best response, and what should the mosque do?
o: RFRA doesn’t bind cities, but the mosque can sue under RLUIPA, which covers state and local land-use decisions.
RFRA is unconstitutional in all of its applications, so the mosque’s only remaining option is a Free Exercise claim under Smith.
The city must satisfy strict scrutiny under RFRA, because Congress enacted RFRA to restore the pre-Smith test for every level of government.
The mosque has no claim, because statutory accommodations that go beyond what the Free Exercise Clause requires violate the Establishment Clause.
e: Rule: RFRA (strict scrutiny for substantial burdens) binds only the federal government after Boerne. RLUIPA (land use and institutionalized persons) binds the states and was upheld in Cutter.
oe: Correct. City of Boerne v. Flores held that RFRA exceeds Congress’s power as applied to state and local governments, though it still binds the federal government. Congress responded with RLUIPA, a narrower statute covering land use and institutionalized persons, which does bind the states.
Boerne invalidated RFRA only as applied to states and localities; it still governs the federal government. And RLUIPA offers a statutory route here.
That was RFRA’s aim, but Boerne held that Congress lacked the power to impose it on states and localities.
Cutter v. Wilkinson unanimously upheld RLUIPA. Government may accommodate religion beyond what Free Exercise requires, though courts weigh the burdens on others.
topic: Establishment, funding, and RFRA — RFRA · Boerne · RLUIPA

q: After a mass shooting at its high school, a town bars, for one year, any “demonstration promoting private firearm ownership” within 500 feet of the school memorial. It finds that such demonstrations would inflict severe emotional trauma on surviving students and families. A gun-rights group is denied permission to hold a silent 20-minute vigil on the public sidewalk across from the memorial. The town argues that the ordinance is a reasonable time, place, and manner rule. How should the court rule?
o: For the group: the ordinance turns on the vigil’s message, and trauma to people who can avoid a brief vigil doesn’t justify suppression.
For the town, because limiting the ban to one year and one location makes it a content-neutral time, place, and manner rule.
For the town, because the survivors of a recent tragedy are a captive audience whose sensibilities the government may protect.
For the town, because protecting the survivors of a mass shooting from deeply offensive speech is a compelling interest that satisfies strict scrutiny.
e: Rule: Collin and Mosley: government may not restrict a peaceful demonstration because of its message, even one that traumatizes listeners. Listener protection is limited to the home and truly captive audiences.
oe: Correct. As in Collin v. Smith, the town objects to who is demonstrating and what they say, not to time, place, or manner, so the ordinance is content-based, and in fact viewpoint-based. Government has no power to restrict expression because of its message (Mosley). Psychic trauma that flows from the ideas themselves doesn’t justify suppression, and residents who can avoid the area for twenty minutes aren’t a captive audience.
A rule limited in time and place is still content-based if it applies only to speech with a particular message. Only gun-rights demonstrations are barred.
Captive-audience protection is reserved for intrusions into the home and truly inescapable settings. A sidewalk vigil is avoidable, just as Skokie residents could avoid Village Hall.
Collin rejected the trauma rationale. The shock comes from the ideas themselves, and offense isn’t a basis for suppressing speech.
topic: Content discrimination and categories — Collin v. Smith · offense and trauma

q: A state statute makes it a crime to “encourage or induce” anyone under 21 to buy vaping products. Lyle, a convenience-store owner, is convicted after handing high-school students free coupons redeemable for vape cartridges at his store. He moves to dismiss, arguing that the statute is facially overbroad because it would let the state prosecute a parent who tells a 20-year-old child, “Try vaping instead of smoking.” What should the court do?
o: Read “encourage or induce” as terms of art for soliciting or facilitating a specific unlawful purchase, then reject the challenge because the remaining protected applications aren’t realistic or substantial.
Dismiss the challenge without reaching the merits, because Lyle’s own conduct is unprotected, so he can’t assert the rights of others.
Strike down the statute, because one realistic protected application is enough to invalidate a law that reaches speech.
Uphold the statute only if the state shows that it has no unconstitutional applications.
e: Rule: Hansen: construe the statute first (avoidance). Overbreadth requires a realistic, substantial, lopsided amount of protected speech relative to the law’s legitimate sweep, and it lets litigants assert others’ rights.
oe: Correct. Under Hansen, the court first construes the statute, adopting any fairly possible constitutional reading (constitutional avoidance). As criminal-law terms of art, “encourage or induce” reach only intentional solicitation and facilitation of specific unlawful acts, not general advice. Overbreadth requires realistic unconstitutional applications that are substantial relative to the law’s plainly legitimate sweep.
Overbreadth is the exception that lets a litigant whose own speech is unprotected assert others’ rights. Lyle may bring the challenge; it fails on the merits.
Overbreadth is “strong medicine.” The protected applications must be substantial relative to the law’s legitimate sweep, and the ratio must be lopsided.

That inverts the test. An ordinary facial challenge requires the challenger to show that a law has no valid applications (Salerno); overbreadth asks whether the protected applications are substantial.
topic: Overbreadth and vagueness — Hansen · overbreadth and construction

q: At a rally of about 200 angry residents outside the city water department, which has just announced a steep rate hike, a speaker points at the building’s glass doors and shouts, “They’re robbing you blind. Go in there right now and smash every computer they’ve got!” Several people immediately rush the doors and break the windows. The speaker is prosecuted under a statute punishing speech “directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it.” Is the conviction constitutional?
o: Yes: the speaker urged an agitated crowd at the scene to break the law at once.
No, because criticism of a government agency is core political speech, which can’t be punished however it is expressed.
No, because incitement requires proof that the speaker personally took part in the lawless action.
Yes, because any speech that creates a clear and present danger of property damage may be punished.
e: Rule: Brandenburg: advocacy of law violation may be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce it.
oe: Correct. All four Brandenburg elements are present. The words were directed to inciting, the action was imminent (“right now”), it was lawless (smashing property), and it was likely given the crowd’s mood and location. This is preparing a group for violent action and steeling it to such action, not abstract advocacy.
A political subject doesn’t immunize incitement. Brandenburg allows punishment when its elements are met, as they are here.
Incitement punishes speech that produces imminent lawless action. The speaker need not take part.
Right result, wrong test. Brandenburg replaced the older clear-and-present-danger formulation with requirements of intent, imminence, and likelihood.
topic: Incitement — Brandenburg · all four elements

q: During a bitter strike, a small group of union supporters marches peacefully on the public sidewalk outside a factory. About 40 replacement workers gather, jeering and throwing a few empty cups. Twenty police officers are on hand and keep the groups apart. After an hour, the officer in charge orders the marchers to disperse “before someone gets hurt” and arrests them when they refuse. Are their disorderly-conduct convictions valid?
o: No, because peaceful speakers can’t be punished for a hostile crowd’s reaction when the police can control the crowd.
Yes, because police may order a demonstration to disperse as soon as onlookers begin to show signs of hostility toward the speakers.
Yes, because the marchers’ presence amounted to fighting words directed at the replacement workers.
No, because labor picketing receives greater constitutional protection than other political speech.
e: Rule: No heckler’s veto (Cox; Edwards): peaceful speakers can’t be punished because a hostile audience might turn violent when the police can control it.
oe: Correct. Under Cox v. Louisiana and Edwards v. South Carolina, there is no heckler’s veto. The marchers were peaceful and twenty officers kept order, so the government had to protect the speakers rather than silence them because of their audience.
That would hand opponents a veto over speech. A dispersal order is justified, if at all, only when the police can’t control the hostile crowd.
Fighting words are face-to-face personal insults likely to provoke immediate violence. A peaceful march isn’t a direct personal insult.
The marchers win under the heckler’s-veto rule, not because labor speech has special status.
topic: Fighting words and hostile audiences — Hostile audiences · no heckler’s veto

q: A county prosecutor, angered by a weekly newspaper’s series accusing the sheriff of taking bribes, obtains a court order barring the paper from publishing “any further article about the sheriff’s office” until a defamation suit is resolved. The paper argues that the order is unconstitutional. The prosecutor responds that the paper would owe damages anyway if the articles were defamatory, so the order merely moves the consequences earlier. Which is the best answer?
o: It is a prior restraint, presumptively invalid; possible defamation liability later is a reason to wait, not to restrain.
The order is valid because defamation is unprotected, so restraining it in advance costs nothing.
The order is valid because it is temporary and will lift once the suit is resolved.
The order is invalid only because a prosecutor, rather than the sheriff in his own defamation lawsuit, asked the court to issue it.
e: Rule: Prior restraints (Near): injunctions or licensing that stop speech in advance carry a heavy presumption of invalidity. Subsequent punishment is the ordinary remedy.
oe: Correct. Stopping speech before it occurs is far more suspect than punishing it afterward. Near v. Minnesota reversed a similar injunction against a paper accusing officials of corruption, stressing the Framers’ special hostility to prior restraints. If an article proves defamatory, the remedy is subsequent liability.
The order bars all future articles about the sheriff’s office, true or not. A court can’t know in advance which ones will be defamatory, which is one reason prior restraints are disfavored.
Temporary restraints are still presumptively invalid. In the Pentagon Papers case, Justice Black called every moment of restraint a flagrant violation.
Who asks for it doesn’t matter. A judicial order barring publication is a prior restraint regardless of the party seeking it.
topic: Prior restraints — Near v. Minnesota · prior vs. subsequent

q: Over three months, Dev sends a former coworker more than 150 messages, opening a new account each time she blocks him. They include “I see you got a new car” and “You won’t get to ignore me much longer.” Terrified, she moves. Dev is convicted under a stalking statute after the jury is told to convict if a reasonable person would view the messages as threatening. On appeal, Dev says he only wanted her attention. What result?
o: The conviction should be vacated, because the state must also prove that Dev consciously disregarded a substantial risk that his messages would be seen as threatening.
The conviction stands, because a true threat is judged solely by how a reasonable recipient would understand it.
The conviction must be reversed outright, because the state must prove that Dev intended to threaten her.
The conviction stands, because repeated unwanted messages are speech integral to stalking and need no threat analysis.
e: Rule: Counterman: a true threat is a statement a reasonable recipient would see as a serious expression of intent to commit unlawful violence, and the speaker must be at least reckless about that risk.
oe: Correct. Counterman requires an objectively threatening statement plus proof that the speaker was at least reckless. A purely objective instruction is inadequate. The state may retry Dev under the proper standard, and on these facts a jury could well find recklessness. Requiring a culpable mental state gives honest speakers breathing room.
That is the purely objective approach of the Counterman dissent (Barrett and Thomas). The majority added a subjective element.
Intent was the concurrence’s position. The majority chose recklessness, so the remedy is a new trial under that standard, not an acquittal.
The state prosecuted on the theory that the messages were threats, so the true-threats requirements, including the mental-state element, apply.
topic: True threats and speech integral to crime — Counterman · recklessness

q: Four people are prosecuted for things they said or wrote. Whose speech is most clearly unprotected as speech integral to criminal conduct?
o: Bea, who texted a friend during a shoplifting spree, “Clerk just went in back, grab the speakers now.”
Cal, who wrote a newspaper column arguing that shoplifting from large chain stores is morally justified.
Dot, who wrote a best-selling crime novel describing in detail how a character shoplifts from a department store.
Eli, who told a crowd at a rally, “Someday the people will take back everything these stores have stolen from them.”
e: Rule: Speech integral to crime (Giboney): speech that is the crime, offers or solicits illegal acts, or helps commit or conceal one is unprotected. Abstract advocacy of illegality is protected.
oe: Correct. Speech that helps commit a crime, like a lookout’s signal, is part of the crime itself (aiding and abetting). It is unprotected whether written or spoken, under Giboney and its progeny.
Abstract advocacy of illegality stays protected. Cal urged no specific crime and assisted none.
Novels and films that depict crime are protected even if a reader copies them; their authors don’t intend to assist crime.
Advocacy of action at some indefinite future time isn’t incitement under Brandenburg, and it isn’t part of any specific crime.
topic: True threats and speech integral to crime — Speech integral to crime · Giboney

q: A state bans mailing unsolicited advertisements for prescription erectile-dysfunction drugs to residential addresses. It cites two interests: protecting adults from offensive mail and helping parents keep such ads away from their children. A telehealth company challenges the ban. How should the court rule?
o: Strike the ban: offense to adults counts for little outside obscenity, and parents already control their own mail.
Uphold the ban, because commercial advertising about sexual matters falls outside the First Amendment.
Uphold the ban, because under Pacifica the government may regulate material that comes into the home to protect children.
Strike the ban only for households without children, because the parental interest justifies it for families with children.
e: Rule: Bolger: outside obscenity, government can’t shield adults from offensive content, and it can protect kids only without cutting off adults’ access.
oe: Correct. Bolger struck down a similar ban on contraceptive ads. Recipients aren’t a captive audience, and the walk from mailbox to trash can is an acceptable burden. Helping parents is a substantial interest, but parents already control their mail, and the government may not reduce adults to reading only what is fit for children.
The ads are protected speech. Among sexual materials, only obscenity, narrowly defined, is unprotected.
Bolger distinguished Pacifica as narrow. Broadcasting is uniquely pervasive and accessible to children, while mail can be thrown away and parents control it.
The Court didn’t divide the ban by household. The parental interest was insufficient because parents can already manage their own mail.
topic: Immoral speech: protecting adults — Bolger · protecting adults vs. kids

q: A state makes it a crime to sell films depicting real children under 16 in sexual performances. A defendant prosecuted under the law argues that the film he sold isn’t obscene under Miller, because taken as a whole it has serious artistic value, so the law is unconstitutional as applied to him. What result?
o: The conviction stands, because Miller doesn’t govern material made with real children.
The conviction must be reversed, because sexual material is unprotected only if it meets all three Miller prongs.
The conviction stands only if the prosecution proves that the film’s message leads viewers to abuse children.
The conviction must be reversed, because Free Speech Coalition protects sexually explicit works with serious value that involve minors.
e: Rule: Ferber: child pornography made with real children is unprotected even if it isn’t obscene, because its distribution is intrinsically related to the abuse.
oe: Correct. Ferber held that the Miller test doesn’t apply. Distribution is intrinsically related to the abuse of the children used to make the material: it is a permanent record of the abuse, and drying up the market may be the only practical way to stop production. The value of such material is exceedingly modest, if not de minimis.
Ferber created a separate category for child pornography made with real children, and it doesn’t depend on Miller.
Ferber’s rationale is the harm to the real children used in production and the market that drives it, not the message’s effect on viewers.
Free Speech Coalition protected images made without real children. When real children are used, Ferber controls regardless of value.
topic: Immoral speech: protecting kids — Ferber · real children

q: A state requires public high-school students to recite each morning a “Pledge of Civic Devotion” affirming that “our free-market system is the best in the world.” A student refuses on political grounds; she has no religious objection. She is suspended. The state argues that Barnette protects only religious objectors and that, in any event, it may require civics instruction. Which is correct?
o: The suspension is unconstitutional. Barnette rests on freedom of speech, which protects secular objectors, and the state may teach economics but not compel students to profess a belief.
The suspension is valid, because only religious objectors may refuse a compelled pledge, and her objection is political.
The suspension is valid, because the pledge states a claim about economics rather than a political opinion.
The suspension is unconstitutional, but only because the state didn’t offer her a different pledge to recite instead.
e: Rule: Barnette: government may not compel anyone to affirm a belief. The protection rests on speech, so secular objectors are covered. Teaching is permitted; compelling is not.
oe: Correct. Barnette’s holding doesn’t depend on religious views or their sincerity, so secular and political objectors are protected equally. Teaching differs from compelling: the state may teach economics and civics, but no official may prescribe what shall be orthodox in politics and force students to confess it.
Barnette rests on the Speech Clause, not religion, and protects any objector.
Whether one system is “the best in the world” is a matter of opinion, which is exactly what no official may prescribe as orthodox.
Offering another pledge wouldn’t cure the problem. The state may not compel any affirmation of belief.
topic: Foundations and compelled expression — Barnette · secular objectors

q: During her lunch break, a public middle-school math teacher sits alone at a picnic table in the school courtyard, silently reads her Bible, and bows her head for a minute. Students eating nearby can see her. She invites no one to join, and no one does. Worried about appearing to endorse religion, the district orders her to pray only in a closed room. She sues, and the district defends its order as required by the Establishment Clause. How is the court likely to treat that defense?
o: It fails: Kennedy reads the Establishment Clause by history and tradition, and quiet prayer that no student is pressed to join isn’t coercion.
It succeeds, because public schools are policed strictly, so any religious expression by a teacher in view of students counts as government prayer.
It succeeds, because a reasonable observer would think the school endorsed the teacher’s religion.
It fails, but only because middle-school students are old enough to tell what a school permits from what it endorses.
e: Rule: Kennedy: the Establishment Clause is read by history and tradition (Lemon and endorsement are gone). It bars coercion, which requires more than visible religious exercise.
oe: Correct. Kennedy abandoned Lemon and the endorsement test. The Establishment Clause still bars coercion, but coercion requires more than visible religious exercise, and treating any visible prayer by a teacher as coercive would itself show hostility to religion. The clauses are complementary, so the Establishment Clause doesn’t automatically trump free exercise.

Schools are policed strictly against government-sponsored religion, such as school prayer and Bible reading (Engel; Schempp), but individual religious expression by employees and students is still protected (Kennedy).
That is the endorsement test, which Kennedy abandoned along with Lemon.
Age matters, but it isn’t the core of the analysis: the history-and-tradition approach and the absence of any coercion are. The prayer was quiet and personal, and no one joined.
topic: School coercion (Kennedy, Mahmoud) — Kennedy · history, tradition, and coercion

q: A state bans the possession of hallucinogenic mushrooms, with no exceptions. Members of a small church whose sacrament involves eating the mushrooms are prosecuted. They argue that the state must show a compelling interest before applying the ban to a sincere religious practice. What result?
o: It may proceed: the Free Exercise Clause requires no exemption from a neutral, generally applicable law that only incidentally burdens religion.
The prosecution must be dismissed unless the state shows a compelling interest, because the ban substantially burdens a sincere religious practice.
The prosecution must be dismissed, because a sacrament is an expression of religious belief, and belief is absolutely protected.
The prosecution may proceed, but only because the church’s practice isn’t shared by any major religious tradition.
e: Rule: Smith: no Free Exercise exemption from neutral, generally applicable laws. Belief is absolutely protected; religious conduct is not.
oe: Correct. This is Employment Division v. Smith on new facts. Belief is absolutely protected, but religious conduct can collide with neutral laws. Strict scrutiny for every incidental burden would create “a private right to ignore generally applicable laws.” Smith relied on Reynolds (polygamy), Prince (child labor), Braunfeld (Sunday closing), and Gillette (the draft).

That was the pre-Smith approach. A substantial burden alone doesn’t trigger strict scrutiny of a neutral, generally applicable law under the Constitution, though a statute like a state RFRA might require it.
Eating the mushrooms is conduct, not belief. The members may believe anything, but their practices can collide with neutral laws, as peyote use did in Smith.
Courts don’t weigh a faith’s size or popularity. The prosecution proceeds because the law is neutral and generally applicable.
topic: Free Exercise — Employment Division v. Smith

q: During a respiratory-virus surge, a state limits indoor gatherings in private homes, religious or secular, to 10 people. Gyms, hair salons, and big-box stores may operate at half capacity, which often exceeds 10 people. A group that holds weekly 15-person Bible studies in a member’s home sues. The state argues that secular gatherings at home face the same limit, so religion is treated equally. Under Tandon v. Newsom, what is the best analysis?
o: Strict scrutiny applies because comparable secular businesses are treated better, so the state must prove the Bible study is riskier.
The rule is neutral and generally applicable, because the right comparison is to secular gatherings at home, which face the same limit.
The rule is valid, because in a public-health emergency the state may assume that worship carries greater risks than work.
Strict scrutiny applies only if the group shows that the state was motivated by hostility toward religion.
e: Rule: Tandon: strict scrutiny applies whenever any comparable secular activity, judged by risk, is treated more favorably than religious exercise.
oe: Correct. Tandon held that a regulation triggers strict scrutiny whenever it treats any comparable secular activity more favorably than religious exercise. Comparability depends on risk, not on whether the activity also takes place at home, and it doesn’t matter that some secular activities are treated equally badly.
That is the Tandon dissent’s “apples and watermelons” argument. The majority looked to any comparable secular activity.
Tandon said the state “cannot assume the worst when people go to worship but assume the best when people go to work.” It must prove the greater risk.
No showing of hostility is needed. Treating comparable secular activity more favorably is enough to trigger strict scrutiny.
topic: Free Exercise — Tandon v. Newsom · comparable activity

q: A state offers grants to private preschools to replace lead water pipes. It denies a grant to a church-run preschool solely because a church owns it, though the application was otherwise ranked first. Separately, a city gives parents scholarships usable at any accredited preschool, religious or secular, and most parents choose religious ones. Which is correct?
o: Only the pipe-grant denial is unconstitutional.
Both programs are valid, because a state may refuse to fund religious institutions directly while allowing indirect aid.
Both programs are unconstitutional, because each results in public money reaching church-run schools.
The pipe-grant denial is valid, but the scholarship program violates the Establishment Clause because most of the money goes to religious schools.
e: Rule: Zelman: aid that reaches religious schools through genuine private choice is permissible. Trinity Lutheran and Espinoza: a state can’t exclude an entity from a public benefit because it is religious.
oe: Correct. Trinity Lutheran (playground resurfacing) and Espinoza held that a state can’t exclude an otherwise eligible entity from a public benefit solely because it is religious. Zelman held that aid reaching religious schools through parents’ genuine and independent private choice is permissible, even when most parents choose religious schools.
Denying the grant solely because the preschool is religious is the status-based exclusion that Trinity Lutheran and Espinoza forbid.
The scholarship program is valid under Zelman; the money reaches religious schools only through private choice.
Wrong on both counts. The share of parents choosing religious schools doesn’t matter under Zelman, and the pipe-grant denial is status discrimination.
topic: Establishment, funding, and RFRA — Zelman · Trinity Lutheran

q: A state bans the sale of recorded music that “portrays illegal drug use approvingly,” while allowing songs that portray drug use as destructive. The legislature cites studies finding that approving lyrics increase teen drug use. A record label challenges the law. What is the strongest ground for striking it down?
o: It favors one viewpoint about drug use and silences the other, which the government may not do even if the disfavored message causes real harm.
The studies show only correlation, so the state can’t prove that the songs cause drug use.
Music is entertainment rather than political speech, so the law gets rational-basis review, which it fails.
The law is void for vagueness, because whether a song portrays illegal drug use “approvingly” is too subjective to give singers and labels fair notice.
e: Rule: Hudnut: government may not favor one viewpoint and silence the other, even when the disfavored speech causes real harm.
oe: Correct. Hudnut struck down Indianapolis’s ban on sexually explicit material depicting women as subordinate even while accepting that such material causes harm; the harm only showed the power of speech. Viewpoint discrimination is the worst form of content discrimination.
Causation might matter under strict scrutiny, but it misses the central defect: the law takes sides. Hudnut struck the ordinance down even after accepting that the harm was real.
Music is protected speech; it is difficult and dangerous to distinguish politics from entertainment (Brown). The law fails because it discriminates by viewpoint, not under rational-basis review.
Vagueness might be argued, but the clearest and strongest ground is viewpoint discrimination.
topic: Content discrimination and categories — Hudnut · viewpoint discrimination

q: A state makes it a misdemeanor to falsely claim, in any setting, to hold a graduate degree from an accredited university. Fen is convicted for telling people at a neighborhood barbecue that he has a Ph.D. in physics; he sought no job, money, or other benefit. On appeal, which argument best supports Fen?
o: False statements aren’t categorically unprotected. This law targets falsity alone, without fraud or other legally cognizable harm, and counterspeech is an adequate remedy.
Lies about credentials are protected unless they are made to government officials.
The Alvarez plurality opinion is binding precedent, and it struck down every law against false statements.
False statements of fact have no constitutional value and fall within a historically unprotected category, so the law is valid.
e: Rule: Alvarez: there is no general exception for false statements. A content-based ban on lies must be actually necessary, and counterspeech is the usual remedy. A plurality opinion usually isn’t binding.
oe: Correct. Under Alvarez, the cases saying falsehood lacks value involved legally cognizable harms such as defamation or fraud. A law reaching lies anywhere, even at a backyard barbecue, targets “falsity and nothing more” and isn’t “actually necessary.” The remedy for false speech is true speech.
Backward. Lies to officials, such as perjury and false statements to investigators, are among the most clearly punishable, because they cause cognizable harm.
A plurality’s reasoning, joined by fewer than five Justices, usually isn’t binding. And Alvarez didn’t disturb laws against fraud, perjury, or defamation.
Alvarez refused to recognize a general exception for false statements. Only falsehood tied to a cognizable harm, such as fraud, is unprotected.
topic: Content discrimination and categories — Alvarez · false statements

q: Aiming at videos of poached endangered fish, Congress bans the commercial sale of any depiction “of a living fish being hooked, speared, or netted” if that conduct was illegal under federal or state law where the depiction is created or sold. A producer of fishing shows is charged for selling a DVD of lawful Canadian salmon spearing in a state where spearing salmon is illegal. The government promises to prosecute only videos of poaching. What should the court do?
o: Strike it down: its text reaches many videos of lawful fishing, and a promise of prosecutorial restraint can’t save it.
Uphold the statute, because the government’s binding promise to prosecute only poaching videos removes any realistic risk of chilling.
Uphold the statute, because depictions of illegal conduct are speech integral to crime.
Dismiss the facial challenge, because the producer may challenge the statute only as applied to his own video.
e: Rule: Stevens: a statute is overbroad when its realistic protected applications dwarf its legitimate sweep, and the government’s promise to enforce it narrowly doesn’t cure that.
oe: Correct. As in Stevens, the statute’s ordinary meaning sweeps in videos of lawful activity whenever that activity is restricted where the video is sold, and those applications dwarf the poaching market. The First Amendment doesn’t leave us “at the mercy of noblesse oblige”: a prosecutor’s promise doesn’t narrow the law.
Stevens rejected exactly this argument. A promise of restraint doesn’t bind future prosecutors or make an overbroad law constitutional.
Selling a video isn’t part of a crime, and the depicted conduct was lawful where it occurred. Stevens refused to treat depictions of animal cruelty as unprotected.
Overbreadth permits a facial challenge based on a law’s applications to others. Stevens struck down the animal-cruelty statute on exactly that basis.
topic: Overbreadth and vagueness — Stevens · overbreadth and noblesse oblige

q: Gil gives a furious speech in a packed hall denouncing the city’s immigration policy while counterprotesters shout outside, and some scuffles break out. He is convicted of breach of the peace after the jury is instructed that the offense includes speech that “stirs the public to anger, invites dispute, or creates a disturbance.” Which is the best basis for reversal?
o: The instruction let the jury convict for speech that merely stirred anger or invited dispute, which is protected.
Speech about immigration policy is core political speech and can’t support a breach-of-the-peace conviction under any instruction.
The counterprotesters started the scuffles, so their conduct can’t be attributed to Gil.
Breach-of-the-peace statutes are inherently vague, so no conviction under one can stand.
e: Rule: Terminiello: speech can’t be punished for stirring anger, inviting dispute, or creating unrest. An instruction that sweeps in protected speech requires reversal.
oe: Correct. Terminiello reversed on this ground. Speech may best serve its purpose when it induces unrest or stirs people to anger. Start with the law: because the instruction swept in protected speech, the conviction couldn’t stand, whatever the facts might have supported.
Political speech can still be punished if it falls within an unprotected category such as incitement. The defect here was the instruction.
That may be a factual point for the jury, but it isn’t the constitutional defect. The instruction let the jury convict for protected speech.
Overstated. Terminiello turned on the breadth of the jury instruction, not on any holding that breach-of-the-peace laws are void.
topic: Incitement — Terminiello · start with the law

q: Jo walks through the public halls of the state capitol, where schoolchildren are touring, wearing a T-shirt with a fully spelled-out four-letter attack on the state legislature. She speaks to no one. She is convicted under a statute punishing fighting words. The state argues that the shirt was offensive and that children were present. What result?
o: Reversed: the shirt insulted no one present face to face and posed no realistic risk of immediate violence.
Affirmed, because profanity in a government building where children are present is fighting words.
Affirmed, because visitors who can’t easily avoid the capitol’s halls are a captive audience.
Reversed, because the Court has since accepted the Harvard note’s argument and overruled Chaplinsky’s fighting-words category.
e: Rule: Chaplinsky and Cohen: fighting words are direct, face-to-face personal insults likely to provoke immediate violence. Offensive messages addressed to the public at large aren’t fighting words.
oe: Correct. Fighting words (Chaplinsky) are face-to-face personal insults likely to provoke the listener to attack the speaker immediately. In Cohen, a “Fuck the Draft” jacket in a courthouse corridor wasn’t fighting words because no one could reasonably take it as a direct personal insult. The Court hasn’t upheld a restriction on a fighting-words theory since 1942.
Profanity isn’t fighting words just because it offends or because children may see it. The category requires a direct personal insult likely to provoke violence.
As in Cohen, visitors could avert their eyes. Captive-audience protection is narrow.

The note (1993) argued that Chaplinsky should be overruled because it rewards fighting and gives police discretion to punish minorities and critics, but the Court hasn’t overruled it. Jo wins because her shirt isn’t fighting words.
topic: Fighting words and hostile audiences — Fighting words · Chaplinsky and Cohen

q: A newspaper has obtained four sets of classified documents and plans to publish them. The government seeks to enjoin all four publications. Which one is the government most likely to be able to restrain?
o: Current military codes and a naval task force’s sailing date and route into an ongoing war.
An internal history showing that officials misled the public about whether a past war could be won.
Diplomatic cables in which senior officials disparage the leaders of several allied nations by name.
A classified budget showing that an intelligence agency overspent its appropriation by billions of dollars.
e: Rule: Pentagon Papers: prior restraints carry a heavy presumption of invalidity, and generalized national-security claims fail. Only narrow tactical military information (Near’s dictum) might be restrained.
oe: Correct. This fits the narrow category in Near’s wartime dictum (troop numbers and locations, transport sailing dates) and the one the ACLU’s Pentagon Papers brief would allow: tactical military operations, weapons designs, and codes. Even here the government bears a heavy burden, and the Court has never actually upheld such a restraint.
That is the Pentagon Papers. Information bearing on public policy decisions is what the ACLU argued should never be restrained, and the Court denied the injunctions.
Embarrassment and generalized diplomatic harm are the kind of vague “security” claim that failed in the Pentagon Papers case.
This is information about government misconduct that bears on public policy. A general claim of harm doesn’t carry the government’s heavy burden.
topic: Prior restraints — Pentagon Papers · the narrow exception

q: In an online chat, Kip offers to sell another user “real videos of 12-year-olds,” intending the buyer to believe that they show real children. In fact, the files are computer-generated. Kip is prosecuted under a statute that punishes offering material in a manner intended to cause another to believe it is child pornography. He argues that because no real child was involved, Free Speech Coalition protects him. What result?
o: The conviction stands, because an offer to provide contraband is unprotected even if the material isn’t what the offeror claims.
The conviction must be reversed, because Free Speech Coalition holds that sexual material made without any real children is protected speech.
The conviction stands only if the government proves that the files depict real children.
The conviction must be reversed, because the statute punishes promoting ideas about child pornography.
e: Rule: Williams: offers and requests to obtain child pornography are unprotected, even when based on a mistaken or false belief. Abstract advocacy remains protected.
oe: Correct. Williams held that offers to provide and requests to obtain child pornography are categorically unprotected as speech integral to crime, and that the statute could reach offers of material the defendant believes, or intends another to believe, is real. Free Speech Coalition protects virtual images themselves, not offers to traffic in what is represented as real child pornography.
Free Speech Coalition concerned bans on the virtual images. Williams concerned the offer, which is unprotected because of what the speaker represents.
The statute turns on the defendant’s belief or intended belief. Williams upheld it partly because technology makes it nearly impossible to prove which images involve real children.
Williams read “promotes” narrowly. It doesn’t reach advocacy such as “child pornography should be legal,” only recommending particular material with intent to initiate a transfer.
topic: True threats and speech integral to crime — Williams · offers and belief

q: A comedian’s routine full of sexual and excretory expletives reaches the public three ways: (1) it airs at 11 a.m. on an over-the-air AM radio station; (2) it is posted as an on-demand podcast episode labeled “explicit”; and (3) it is printed on T-shirts sold online. A federal agency proposes to sanction all three as indecent. Under Pacifica, which sanction is most defensible?
o: Only the sanction for the morning radio broadcast.
All three, because Pacifica held that indecent speech can be regulated in any medium where children might encounter it.
Only the T-shirts, because indecent words worn in public reach a captive audience.
None of them, because the routine is indecent rather than obscene, and the government may restrict only obscene speech.
e: Rule: Pacifica: the government may regulate indecent but non-obscene broadcasts because broadcasting is uniquely pervasive and accessible to children. The holding is narrow and depends on context and medium.
oe: Correct. Pacifica’s narrow, nuisance-based holding rests on broadcasting’s special features: it is uniquely pervasive, reaches into the home, confronts unconsenting listeners without warning, and is accessible to unsupervised children, and the spectrum is scarce and licensed. A labeled, on-demand podcast and a T-shirt lack those features, and profanity in those media is protected (Cohen).
Pacifica’s holding is narrow and depends on context: time of day, program content, and medium all matter.
Cohen held that viewers can avert their eyes. A T-shirt is the least regulable of the three.

Pacifica is the exception: indecent but non-obscene broadcasts can be regulated because of broadcasting’s special characteristics. It left open other media, an occasional expletive, and criminal prosecution.
topic: Immoral speech: protecting adults — Pacifica · the medium matters

q: Responding to AI image generators, Congress bans creating or distributing any sexually explicit image that “appears to be of a person under 18,” whether or not a real child was involved and whatever the work’s value. A publisher prepares an acclaimed graphic-novel adaptation of a classic coming-of-age novel. One explicit, entirely drawn scene involves two 17-year-old characters. The publisher challenges the ban. What result?
o: It is unconstitutional as applied to images made without real children, because Ferber rests on protecting real children.
The ban is valid, because Ferber holds that sexual depictions of minors are unprotected regardless of obscenity or value.
The ban is valid, because drawn and computer-generated images are not speech.
The ban is valid if the graphic novel, taken as a whole, lacks serious value, because Miller supplies the test for all sexual images of minors.
e: Rule: Free Speech Coalition: Ferber doesn’t extend to sexually explicit images made without real children, such as virtual images or adult look-alikes.
oe: Correct. Free Speech Coalition struck down a ban on images that “appear to” depict minors. Virtual images and adult look-alikes don’t involve the abuse of real children that justified Ferber. The ban also ignores value: a work’s artistic merit doesn’t depend on a single explicit scene, and teenage sexuality is an enduring literary theme (Juliet is 13).
Ferber’s holding is tied to real children. It doesn’t extend to images made without them.
Drawn and computer-generated images are speech. The question is whether they fall within an unprotected category, and Free Speech Coalition says they don’t when no real child is involved.
The ban requires no Miller findings, which is part of why it fails. Material that is actually obscene under Miller could be banned, but this statute isn’t limited to it.
topic: Immoral speech: protecting kids — Free Speech Coalition · no real children

q: A federal statute makes it a crime for commercial websites to post material “harmful to minors” unless they verify each visitor’s age with a credit card. The plaintiffs show that home content filters, which parents can install, block such material at least as well, including from foreign sites. The government offers no evidence that the statute would work better than filters. Under Ashcroft v. ACLU (Ashcroft II), how should the court rule on a motion for a preliminary injunction?
o: Grant it: under strict scrutiny the government must prove filters would be less effective, and it offered no evidence.
Deny it, because protecting children from sexual material is compelling, and the statute need only be reasonably tailored.
Deny it, because the plaintiffs must prove that filters work perfectly before they count as an alternative.
Grant it, because the government’s power over sexual material stops at what is obscene for adults.
e: Rule: Ashcroft II: under strict scrutiny, a content-based law that burdens adults’ access fails if less restrictive alternatives such as filters would be at least as effective, and the government must prove they aren’t.
oe: Correct. Ashcroft II applied strict scrutiny to COPA, a content-based criminal law that burdened adults’ access to protected speech. Filters restrict at the receiving end, don’t require adults to identify themselves, and criminalize no speech; they may also work better because they block foreign sites. The burden was on the government, and it offered no specific evidence.
Under strict scrutiny a law must use the least restrictive means, and the government must show that alternatives are less effective.
Filters are imperfect, but Ashcroft II put the burden on the government to show that its law works better.
States may keep minors from material that is obscene as to them (Ginsberg). The problem was the burden on adults and the availability of less restrictive alternatives.
topic: Immoral speech: protecting kids — Ashcroft II · filters

q: A state requires every passenger car to display a windshield sticker, issued at inspection, bearing the state motto “Faith, Family, Freedom” and the car’s inspection number. Covering the motto carries a fine. An owner who objects to the motto tapes over it but leaves the inspection number visible. The state cites two interests: helping police spot uninspected cars and fostering state pride. Which is correct?
o: The requirement is unconstitutional as applied, because the number alone serves identification, and state pride is an ideological interest that can’t force him to carry the motto.
The requirement is valid, because displaying a sticker is passive and far less intrusive than reciting a pledge.
The requirement is valid, because the motto is like “In God We Trust” on the currency that everyone must carry.
The requirement is valid, because the state may compel factual disclosures, such as inspection numbers and nutrition labels.
e: Rule: Wooley: the state may not require people to display its ideological message on their property. Identification doesn’t require the motto, and ideological interests can’t justify compelled display. Currency is distinguishable.
oe: Correct. Wooley v. Maynard struck down New Hampshire’s “Live Free or Die” plate requirement. Passive display still counts, because the car becomes a mobile billboard. Identification can be achieved without the motto, so the law isn’t narrowly tailored, and an interest in spreading an ideology can’t outweigh the right not to be its courier.
Wooley said the difference between carrying a motto and saluting a flag is only one of degree.
Wooley’s footnote 15 distinguished currency: it is carried privately and isn’t associated with the bearer, while a car is displayed to the public and identified with its owner.
Compelled factual and commercial disclosures (a Chapter 8 topic) are different. The motto is an ideological message, not a factual disclosure, and the owner left the inspection number visible.
topic: Foundations and compelled expression — Wooley v. Maynard · compelled display

q: A required 11th-grade social-studies course includes a two-week unit in which students read short descriptive excerpts from the Bible, the Quran, the Bhagavad Gita, and humanist essays, then write a paper comparing how the traditions approach death. Teachers are told not to endorse or criticize any tradition. The district grants no opt-outs from any part of its curriculum. Evangelical parents, citing Mahmoud, seek an opt-out. What is the district’s strongest response?
o: Unlike Mahmoud’s books, this unit is descriptive, aimed at older students, corrects no one, and asks no one to adopt a view.
Mahmoud is limited to curricula about sexuality and gender identity, so its reasoning doesn’t reach a unit on the world’s religions.
Granting an opt-out would itself establish religion by favoring the objecting parents’ faith.
Mahmoud’s majority held that mere exposure to ideas contrary to a family’s faith can’t burden religious exercise.
e: Rule: Mahmoud’s burden inquiry is fact-intensive (beliefs, content, age, context). Descriptive material for older students with no correction looks like mere exposure. The rule must apply neutrally, whichever side objects.
oe: Correct. Mahmoud stressed that the inquiry is fact-intensive: the beliefs, the nature of the curriculum, the children’s age, and the context. Older students (as in Kennedy) studying descriptive material, with no correction or labeling of objections, looks more like the mere exposure Mahmoud didn’t treat as a burden. And with no other opt-outs, the policy stays generally applicable under Smith.
The casebook stresses that rules must apply neutrally to similar facts, whichever side wins. Mahmoud’s test turns on the burden on religious upbringing, not the topic.
Government may accommodate religion beyond what Free Exercise requires (the first sense of “play in the joints”), and Mahmoud itself required opt-outs.
That is the Mahmoud dissent’s position. The majority found a burden from exposure combined with normative content, young children, and the correction of dissent.
topic: School coercion (Kennedy, Mahmoud) — Mahmoud’s limits · world religions

q: A state civil-rights commission finds that a print-shop owner violated the public-accommodations law by refusing, on religious grounds, to print invitations for a same-sex wedding. At the public hearing, one commissioner says that “religion has been used to justify every kind of discrimination in history” and that the owner “can believe what he wants at home, but not in business.” No other commissioner disavows the remarks. The commission earlier found that three print shops acted lawfully when they refused to print flyers opposing same-sex marriage. What is the owner’s strongest argument on appeal?
o: The commission didn’t apply the law neutrally: it showed hostility to his beliefs and treated his objection worse than comparable objections.
Public-accommodations laws can’t constitutionally be applied to any business owner who objects on religious grounds to serving same-sex weddings.
The public-accommodations law is invalid because it isn’t neutral on its face.
Smith entitles him to an exemption because printing invitations is expressive.
e: Rule: Masterpiece Cakeshop: even a neutral law must be applied neutrally. Official hostility, or treating a religious objection worse than comparable objections, violates Free Exercise. The holding is narrow.
oe: Correct. Masterpiece Cakeshop set aside a similar order. Even a neutral law must be applied neutrally. Unrebutted remarks disparaging religious justifications, and the more favorable treatment of comparable shops, showed the commission didn’t give his claim neutral consideration.

Masterpiece was narrow. The Court didn’t resolve the tension between antidiscrimination law and the First Amendment, and it said states can generally protect gay persons’ equal access to goods and services.
Nothing suggests that the law is facially non-neutral. The problem was hostility and disparate treatment in applying it.
Smith denies exemptions from neutral, generally applicable laws. The owner wins on hostility, not on a Smith exemption.
topic: Free Exercise — Masterpiece Cakeshop · hostility

q: A state enacts two laws. Law 1 bars ordained clergy of any faith from serving as officers in the state’s National Guard. Law 2, a neutral and generally applicable rule, requires every child to attend an accredited school through age 18, and Amish parents seek an exemption after the eighth grade. Under Employment Division v. Smith, how should a court analyze them?
o: Law 1 is invalid because it imposes a disability based on religious status, and Smith would treat the Amish claim as a hybrid of free exercise and the parents’ right to direct their children’s education.
Both laws are valid, because under Smith no religious claimant may obtain relief from a law that applies to everyone.
Law 1 is valid because it treats clergy of every faith alike, and Law 2 must be applied to the Amish without exception.
Both laws are invalid, because Smith requires strict scrutiny whenever a law substantially burdens a sincere religious practice.
e: Rule: Smith: government may never regulate belief as such, impose disabilities based on religious status, punish doctrines, or take sides in religious disputes. Smith explained past exemptions like Yoder as hybrid-rights cases.
oe: Correct. Smith said government may never impose special disabilities based on religious status, regulate belief as such, punish doctrines it thinks false, or take sides in religious disputes. Smith explained Yoder, which exempted Amish children from schooling past eighth grade, as a hybrid case pairing free exercise with parents’ right to direct their children’s upbringing. Mahmoud now treats that kind of burden as its own trigger for strict scrutiny.
Law 1 doesn’t apply to everyone; it singles out clergy by their religious status. And Smith preserved hybrid claims like Yoder’s.
Treating all faiths alike doesn’t cure a disability based on religious status. And the Amish claim falls within the Yoder line.
That was the pre-Smith rule, which Smith rejected for neutral, generally applicable laws.
topic: Free Exercise — Smith’s limits · status and hybrid rights

q: Four practices are challenged under the Establishment Clause. Which is most likely to be held unconstitutional?
o: A public elementary school’s practice of opening each day with a teacher-led nondenominational prayer that students may sit out.
A 60-year-old granite monument displaying the Ten Commandments among other historical markers on the grounds of a state capitol building.
A state legislature’s practice of opening its sessions with a brief prayer by a rotating guest chaplain.
The federal government’s printing of “In God We Trust” on its currency.
e: Rule: The Establishment Clause bars an official religion, coercion, benefits only for religious entities, favoring one sect, and school indoctrination. Schools are policed most strictly (Engel), while longstanding displays, legislative prayer, and the national motto are allowed on historical grounds.
oe: Correct. Public schools are policed most strictly because they are uniquely coercive and children are impressionable. Engel v. Vitale struck down even nonmandatory school prayer.
Longstanding religious displays are generally allowed on historical grounds. Van Orden v. Perry upheld the Texas Capitol monument, 5–4.
Short legislative prayers are generally upheld under the history-and-tradition approach.
The circuits uphold the national motto on currency (Newdow v. Peterson).
topic: Establishment, funding, and RFRA — Establishment Clause core · schools vs. tradition

q: A family-owned, closely held restaurant chain whose owners object on religious grounds sues under RFRA for an exemption from a federal regulation requiring employer health plans to cover IVF treatment. The government argues that (1) a for-profit corporation can’t exercise religion, and (2) any statutory exemption that goes beyond what the Free Exercise Clause requires would violate the Establishment Clause. How should the court treat these arguments?
o: Reject both, but weigh the costs to employees: closely held corporations may invoke RFRA, and accommodation is permissible.
Accept the first: for-profit corporations exist to make money, so they can’t bring RFRA claims.
Accept the second: an exemption not compelled by the Free Exercise Clause favors religion and so establishes it.
Reject both, and hold that the costs to employees become irrelevant once the owners show that the regulation substantially burdens their religion.
e: Rule: Hobby Lobby: RFRA protects closely held for-profit corporations. Cutter: accommodation beyond what Free Exercise requires is permissible (play in the joints), but courts weigh the burdens on third parties.
oe: Correct. Burwell v. Hobby Lobby (5–4) held that RFRA protects closely held for-profit corporations with religious owners. The first sense of “play in the joints,” still alive, lets government accommodate religion beyond what Free Exercise requires (Cutter upheld RLUIPA unanimously), but courts must take account of the burdens an accommodation places on nonbeneficiaries, like these employees.
Hobby Lobby rejected that argument for closely held corporations whose owners hold religious beliefs.
Cutter upheld RLUIPA’s accommodations. Accommodation beyond what Free Exercise requires is permissible, within limits.
Third-party costs matter. Cutter said courts must consider burdens on nonbeneficiaries, and Hobby Lobby illustrates accommodation’s costs to third parties.
topic: Establishment, funding, and RFRA — Hobby Lobby · accommodation and its costs

q: A state enacts four new laws. Which one can be upheld without surviving strict scrutiny, because it reaches only speech within a historically recognized unprotected category?
o: A ban on raising charity donations through knowingly false claims about where the money goes.
A ban on speech demeaning people because of their religion, which the legislature found to have negligible value and high social costs.
A ban on selling videos depicting animals being tortured or killed, if that conduct is illegal where the video is sold.
A ban on falsely claiming to have won a military medal, whether or not the speaker seeks any benefit.
e: Rule: Stevens: content-based laws are presumptively invalid unless the speech falls within a historically recognized unprotected category. Courts may not create new categories by balancing value against harm.
oe: Correct. Fraud is among the historically unprotected categories, along with incitement, fighting words, true threats, speech integral to crime, child pornography, obscenity, and defamation in some circumstances. A law limited to knowingly false solicitations fits that tradition.
Hate speech is generally protected. And under Stevens, a legislature can’t create a new category by finding that a kind of speech’s costs outweigh its value.
Stevens refused to recognize depictions of animal cruelty as an unprotected category, because there is no tradition of banning them.
Alvarez refused to recognize a general exception for false statements. Lies that cause no legally cognizable harm remain protected.
topic: Content discrimination and categories — Stevens · the historical categories

q: Nia is charged under a statute making it a crime to “knowingly provide expert advice or assistance” to a designated foreign terrorist organization, after she taught the group’s members how to write press releases soliciting donations for weapons. She argues that the statute is void for vagueness because it is unclear whether it would cover a professor giving a general lecture on international law, and because it will often be hard to prove what a defendant knew. Which is the best response?
o: Vagueness looks mainly to her own conduct, which is clearly covered, and proof problems are for the reasonable-doubt standard.
The statute is void for vagueness, because the existence of close cases shows that it fails to give fair notice.
She may rely on the professor’s situation under the vagueness doctrine, just as a litigant may rely on others’ rights under overbreadth.
Vagueness is a First Amendment doctrine, so it applies only to statutes that regulate speech.
e: Rule: Vagueness (Due Process): a law is void if it fails to give fair notice or invites seriously discriminatory enforcement, judged mainly by the litigant’s own conduct. Close cases and problems of proof don’t make a law vague.
oe: Correct. Vagueness, which comes from the Due Process Clause, asks whether a law gives fair notice or invites seriously discriminatory enforcement. A litigant whose own conduct is clearly covered generally can’t complain about hypotheticals (Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project). And Williams held that difficulty proving a fact isn’t vagueness; vagueness concerns indeterminacy about what fact must be proved, like “annoying.”
Williams rejected this. Close cases are resolved by the reasonable-doubt standard, not by voiding the law.
Overbreadth lets litigants assert third parties’ rights. Vagueness looks mainly to the litigant’s own conduct.
Vagueness comes from the Due Process Clause and applies to criminal laws generally, though it shares overbreadth’s goal of preventing chilling.
topic: Overbreadth and vagueness — Vagueness · fair notice and own conduct

q: At 9 p.m., Rae, a livestreamer, tells 20,000 viewers: “The councilman who voted for the rezoning lives at 14 Elm Street. Someone needs to go there tonight and make sure he never forgets it.” Within an hour, three viewers who live nearby throw rocks through his windows. Rae is prosecuted for incitement. Her lawyer argues that her audience was scattered online rather than gathered at the scene, and that she never mentioned violence. Which fact most strengthens the prosecution’s case under Brandenburg?
o: She named a specific target and address and set a time frame of that night, and viewers acted within the hour.
Her audience was so large that some viewers were statistically bound to act violently.
Her remark was insulting and deeply offensive to the councilman.
She had posted a week earlier that the rezoning was “an act of war on our neighborhood” and that residents should “fight back.”
e: Rule: Brandenburg: imminence and specificity separate incitement from protected advocacy of future or conditional action (Hess). An online audience can make likelihood harder to prove, but a specific target and time frame support every element.
oe: Correct. Brandenburg requires intent, imminence, and likelihood. A named target and address, the word “tonight,” and swift action support imminence and likelihood, and the specificity supports intent. That distinguishes this from advocacy of action at some indefinite later time (Hess). An online audience makes likelihood harder to prove, but not impossible.
Audience size alone doesn’t show that the speaker intended imminent lawless action, and punishing speakers for their most volatile listeners risks a heckler’s-veto effect.
Offensiveness doesn’t make speech incitement. The elements are intent, imminence, lawless action, and likelihood.
Heated rhetoric about a public issue is protected advocacy. It might shed some light on intent, but it is far weaker evidence than the specific call to act that night.
topic: Incitement — Incitement online · imminence and specificity

q: After R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul, a city wants to punish people who hurl slurs at others because of their race. Which ordinance is most likely to survive a facial First Amendment challenge?
o: One that punishes all fighting words, whatever their subject.
One that punishes fighting words based on race, color, creed, religion, or gender.
One that punishes only fighting words based on race, because racial insults cause unique harm.
One that punishes displaying any symbol that arouses anger or resentment in others on the basis of race, whether or not it amounts to fighting words.
e: Rule: R.A.V.: government may ban an entire unprotected category for the reason it is proscribable, but it may not single out a subset by topic or viewpoint. Unprotected categories aren’t “invisible to the Constitution.”
oe: Correct. R.A.V. allows government to ban an entire unprotected category because of what makes it proscribable (here, the tendency to provoke immediate violence), but not to single out a subset by topic or viewpoint. A ban on all fighting words avoids that problem.
That is St. Paul’s ordinance as construed, which R.A.V. struck down as a topic-based subset of fighting words.
Narrowing the subset further doesn’t help. Singling out race-based fighting words is still discrimination by topic within the category.
That reaches protected speech: arousing anger or resentment isn’t enough. The ordinance is both content-based and overbroad.
topic: Fighting words and hostile audiences — R.A.V. · subsets of a category

q: As a condition of employment, a former CIA officer signed an agreement to submit anything she writes about the agency for prepublication review. She publishes a memoir without submitting it; it contains no classified information. The government sues to impose a constructive trust on her royalties. Meanwhile, a newspaper that independently learned the same facts plans to publish them, and the government seeks to enjoin the paper. Which is the best prediction?
o: The government will likely win against the officer, based on her agreement, but not against the newspaper, which keeps the heavy presumption against prior restraints.
The government will lose both, because the Pentagon Papers case adopted Justice Black’s view that every prior restraint is a flagrant violation.
The government will win both, because the secrecy agreement binds anyone who publishes information about the CIA.
The government will lose against the officer, because her memoir contained no classified information.
e: Rule: Secrecy agreements (Marchetti; Snepp): government employees can be held to contractual prepublication review. The press, which signed nothing, keeps the heavy presumption against prior restraints.
oe: Correct. Snepp and Marchetti rested on CIA employees’ contractual secrecy agreements, and Snepp imposed a constructive trust on royalties even though the book contained no classified information. A newspaper that signed nothing gets the full protection of the presumption against prior restraints (Near; the Pentagon Papers).
Black wrote only for himself and Justice Douglas. The per curiam held that the government hadn’t met its heavy burden, and the secrecy cases rest on contract.
Only the officer agreed to prepublication review. The newspaper is a stranger to the contract.
In Snepp, breaching the review agreement was enough to support the remedy, whether or not the book contained classified information.
topic: Prior restraints — Secrecy agreements · Snepp and Marchetti

q: After losing a student-government election, Ula, a high-school senior, posts on her public account: “If they don’t recount those ballots I’m going to burn this school to the ground, lol.” Her friends reply with laughing reactions. The principal has no reason to think she has any interest in fire or weapons but refers her for prosecution under a threats statute. Which is her strongest defense?
o: Read in context, the post is hyperbole that a reasonable recipient wouldn’t take seriously, so it isn’t a true threat.
The prosecution must prove that she intended to threaten, as the Counterman majority required.
Social-media posts can’t be true threats, because online speech lacks the context needed to judge them.
