The Counterman dissent’s purely objective test would protect her, but the majority’s added recklessness requirement would not.
e: Rule: A true threat must be a serious expression of intent to commit unlawful violence, judged in context; jests and hyperbole aren’t threats. In Counterman, the majority required recklessness, the concurrence intent, and the dissent an objective test only.
oe: Correct. “True” in true threats excludes jests and hyperbole, like “I’ll kill you if you leave dirty dishes in the sink.” The context (a lost election, “lol,” laughing replies, no history of violence) shows that a reasonable recipient wouldn’t take the post as a serious threat. If a statement isn’t objectively threatening, the mental-state question never arises.
The Counterman majority required recklessness; intent was the concurrence’s view (Sotomayor, joined in part by Gorsuch). And the stronger defense is that the post isn’t a threat at all.
Counterman itself involved Facebook messages. The concurrence noted that online speech can lack context, but online statements can still be true threats.

Backward. Every opinion requires the statement to be objectively threatening; the dissent (Barrett and Thomas) would have stopped there. The majority’s recklessness requirement adds a protection rather than removing one.
topic: True threats and speech integral to crime — True threats · jest, hyperbole, and the opinions

q: A publisher sells a detailed online manual for building untraceable pipe bombs, marketed to the general public alongside its books on chemistry and pyrotechnics. A buyer uses it to build a bomb that injures his neighbor, who sues the publisher for aiding and abetting. Unlike the publisher in Rice v. Paladin, this publisher has stipulated to nothing and denies any intent to assist crime. What is the publisher’s strongest argument?
o: Absent evidence beyond the text that it meant to help criminals, a general-audience manual isn’t unprotected aiding and abetting.
Publishers are immune from aiding-and-abetting liability for what they print.
Technical instructions are protected only when they also contain political or ideological advocacy, which this manual lacks entirely.
The neighbor must also prove that the manual satisfies the Brandenburg test for incitement.
e: Rule: Rice v. Paladin: publishing can be unprotected aiding and abetting when the publisher intended to assist criminals and the material was used as intended. Without such evidence, a general-audience instructional work is likely protected.
oe: Correct. Paladin turned on extraordinary stipulations that the publisher intended to assist murderers and knew the book would be used for murder, along with the book’s exhortations and lack of any legitimate purpose. Evidence of intent will almost never exist without such stipulations. A general-audience manual with possible legitimate readers (engineers, researchers, novelists) is closer to the copycat cases, and Stevens bars creating a new category by balancing.
Paladin rejected any such immunity. Publishing that aids and abets a crime is unprotected when the intent and the use are shown.
There is no such rule. Technical information can be protected speech; the issue is whether the publisher intended to facilitate crime.
Aiding and abetting is a different theory, speech integral to crime, not incitement. The issue is intent and use, not imminence.
topic: True threats and speech integral to crime — Rice v. Paladin · the bomb manual

q: A county prosecutes a bookstore for selling an illustrated novel about a woman’s sexual awakening. The judge instructs the jury that the book is obscene if (1) it arouses normal, healthy sexual desire in the average reader, (2) any scene depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way, and (3) the charged passages lack serious literary value. What is the most serious error in the instruction?
o: It judges parts instead of the whole work and treats normal sexual interest as prurient.
It should have asked the jury whether the novel offends most of the county’s adult residents.
It should have required the prosecution to prove that the novel depicts minors in sexual conduct.
It should have let the jury convict if the novel conveys a degrading view of women, whatever its value.
e: Rule: Miller: material is obscene only if, taken as a whole, it appeals to the prurient (shameful or morbid) interest under community standards, depicts specifically defined sexual conduct in a patently offensive way, and lacks serious value.
oe: Correct. Miller requires that the work, taken as a whole, appeal to the prurient interest and, taken as a whole, lack serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. Prong (c) protects valuable works even if some scenes are explicit. And prurient interest means a shameful or morbid interest in sex, not a normal one (Brockett v. Spokane Arcades).
Offensiveness alone isn’t the test. Miller requires all three prongs, including prurient appeal and a lack of serious value.
That describes the child-pornography category (Ferber). Obscenity covers sexual material about adults that meets all three Miller prongs.

That was the theory of the Indianapolis ordinance in Hudnut, which didn’t track Miller (no prurient interest, community standards, or work-as-a-whole inquiry, and value was irrelevant). The court struck it down as viewpoint discrimination.
topic: Immoral speech: protecting adults — Miller · the obscenity test

q: A classmate says: “Paxton silently overruled Ashcroft II. In 2004 filters defeated an age-verification law, and in 2025 they didn’t.” Which response best describes how the Paxton majority itself explained the different results?
o: It used intermediate scrutiny because age verification only incidentally burdens adults; the earlier laws effectively banned adult access.
Paxton held that sexually explicit material is unprotected for adults as well as for minors, so it applied only rational-basis review to the law.
Paxton applied strict scrutiny but found that filters had become less effective than age verification since 2004.
Paxton expressly overruled both Ashcroft II and Reno v. ACLU.
e: Rule: Paxton: age-verification laws for material obscene as to minors get intermediate scrutiny because their burden on adults is incidental. The Court distinguished Reno and Ashcroft II as effective bans on adult access.
oe: Correct. Paxton held that a law requiring age verification to keep minors from speech that is obscene as to them gets intermediate scrutiny, because any burden on adults is incidental (relying on Ginsberg). It framed Reno and Ashcroft II as involving effective bans on adult speech and stressed how much the internet has changed. Under intermediate scrutiny, less restrictive alternatives like filters don’t defeat a legitimate legislative choice. Whether that fully squares with Ashcroft II is the open question.
Paxton rejected rational-basis review because adults have a real, if incidentally burdened, right to the material.
Paxton applied intermediate scrutiny, which it called “deferential but not toothless.” That lower standard, not new facts about filters, is why filters lost.
The Court distinguished those cases rather than overruling them.
topic: Immoral speech: protecting kids — Paxton · did it overrule Ashcroft II?

q: A state university requires graduates attending commencement to stand with a hand over the heart during the national anthem. Graduates who refuse are escorted out before they cross the stage; their diplomas are mailed later. A graduate wants to stay seated to protest U.S. foreign policy. The university argues that attendance is optional and that a rational basis supports promoting patriotism. Which response best supports the graduate?
o: The gesture is a form of utterance compelled by the state, restricting it requires more than a rational basis, and forcing a choice between a major life event and the gesture is itself coercive.
Adults can’t be coerced by a ceremony they choose to attend, so the requirement is constitutional.
Standing is conduct rather than speech, so the First Amendment doesn’t apply.
The requirement is invalid only if her objection is religious, as the objections in Barnette were.
e: Rule: Barnette: symbolic conduct is a form of utterance, and compelled expression may be required only to prevent grave and immediate danger, not on a rational basis. Forcing a choice between an important event and a compelled gesture still looks coercive.
oe: Correct. Barnette treated the salute as symbolic conduct, “a form of utterance,” and allowed restrictions only to prevent grave and immediate danger, not on a rational basis. Political objectors are protected like religious ones. Optional attendance helps the university, but Mahmoud rejected the “just go elsewhere” answer, and the policy offers no passive option within the ceremony. The case sits below Barnette’s compelled pledge on the coercion spectrum, so it is close.
Adulthood and optional attendance are real differences from Barnette, but adults are protected from compelled expression too; the drivers in Wooley were adults.
Barnette held that symbolic conduct like a salute is a form of utterance. Standing for an anthem is a “confession by act.”
Barnette rests on speech, not religion, so her political objection is protected.
topic: Foundations and compelled expression — Barnette · symbolic conduct at commencement

q: Before each match, a public-university volleyball coach crosses herself and bows her head silently for a few seconds. The athletic director writes in her evaluation, “Your conduct is unmistakably religious, and we can’t have that on the court,” and suspends her. The university argues that its rule against “personal displays during competition” is neutral. Under Kennedy v. Bremerton, how should the court analyze her Free Exercise claim?
o: Strict scrutiny, because the university admitted it acted because her conduct was religious.
The discipline is valid under Smith, because the rule against personal displays applies to every coach.
The discipline is valid, because a coach’s gestures during a game are government speech that the university controls.
The university wins if it shows that spectators could reasonably perceive it as endorsing her faith.
e: Rule: Kennedy: disciplining a public employee’s private religious exercise because it is religious isn’t neutral, and it triggers strict scrutiny.
oe: Correct. In Kennedy, the district admitted that it disciplined the coach partly because his conduct was religious, which made its action not neutral and triggered strict scrutiny. A facially neutral rule doesn’t help when officials say they are acting because of the conduct’s religious character.
Smith covers only neutral and generally applicable laws. An admitted religious motive defeats neutrality.
The Kennedy Court treated the coach’s brief, quiet prayer as private religious exercise, not government speech.
Kennedy abandoned the endorsement test. An Establishment Clause defense requires coercion, and a brief, silent gesture doesn’t supply it.
topic: School coercion (Kennedy, Mahmoud) — Kennedy · admitted religious motive

q: A state requires every schoolchild to attend a series of classroom sessions on online safety, with no exemptions. Parents from a religious community that forbids internet use argue that the sessions interfere with their children’s religious upbringing. Assume the court finds a substantial interference. What is the most accurate statement of the next step?
o: Strict scrutiny applies even though the law is neutral and generally applicable, so the state must show an interest of the highest order, narrowly tailored, in denying these families an exemption.
Smith controls because the law is neutral and generally applicable, so the parents get no exemption.
The parents win without further inquiry, because Mahmoud forbids states from overriding parents’ religious objections.
Rational-basis review applies, because the parental right is unenumerated, and the Court abandoned such rights after Dobbs.
e: Rule: Wrinkle 1 (Yoder; Mahmoud): a substantial interference with parents’ religious upbringing of their children triggers strict scrutiny even under a neutral, generally applicable law. Strict scrutiny requires an interest of the highest order, narrowly tailored to this claimant.
oe: Correct. Under Wrinkle 1 (Yoder; Mahmoud), a substantial interference with parents’ religious upbringing of their children triggers strict scrutiny even under a generally applicable law. Strict scrutiny requires an interest of the highest order, narrowly tailored, judged as to this exemption (Fulton). The burden is on the government, which almost always loses.
Wrinkle 1 is an exception to Smith for parents’ religious education of their children.
Mahmoud applied strict scrutiny, which the government can in theory satisfy, and its burden inquiry is fact-intensive.

Smith explained Yoder as resting partly on an unenumerated parental right, and the Mahmoud Court, wary of such rights after Dobbs, said little about the doctrinal basis. But it still applied strict scrutiny.
topic: Free Exercise — Wrinkle 1 · strict scrutiny

q: A city requires all food-service workers to wear hairnets and bans head coverings that can’t be fully secured. A Sikh line cook is fired for refusing to replace his turban with a hairnet, and he sues under the Free Exercise Clause. Which fact, if proven, would most help the city defend its rule?
o: The rule has no exceptions, covers every kitchen, and was adopted on a health inspector’s advice years before he was hired.
The city has granted waivers to cooks with medical conditions, such as scalp disorders, who can’t tolerate wearing hairnets for a full shift.
The city council discussed the cook’s religion when it voted to keep the rule.
Some scholars of his tradition say the faith doesn’t require a turban in every setting.
e: Rule: Free Exercise checklist: a neutral, generally applicable law requires no exemption (Smith). Exemption systems, favored secular comparators, hostility, or a religious motive trigger strict scrutiny.
oe: Correct. If the rule is neutral and generally applicable, Smith requires no constitutional exemption, and the city needs only a rational basis. Showing that the rule has no exemption system (Fulton) or gerrymandered exceptions (Lukumi), favors no comparable secular activity (Tandon), and reflects no religious motive (Kennedy) or hostility (Masterpiece) keeps it within Smith.
That hurts the city. Exemptions for comparable secular reasons undercut general applicability (Fulton; Tandon).
Evidence that officials focused on his religion suggests hostility or a religious motive, either of which triggers strict scrutiny (Masterpiece; Kennedy).
Courts don’t resolve religious disputes, and beliefs need not be consistent or shared by others (Lukumi; Smith). The question is sincerity, and nothing suggests he is insincere.
topic: Free Exercise — The Free Exercise checklist

q: A state charter-school board rejects a religious organization’s application to open a charter school offering religious instruction, citing the Establishment Clause. The state’s charter schools are created by state law, fully state-funded, supervised by a state board, tuition-free, and open to all. The organization sues, relying on Carson v. Makin. Which statement best describes the issue?
o: If charter schools are public, a religious charter violates the Establishment Clause; if they’re private, excluding religious applicants violates Free Exercise. The Supreme Court split 4–4 on the question.
Carson squarely holds that states must approve religious charter schools on the same terms as secular ones.
In Drummond the Supreme Court held that charter schools are public schools that may not offer religious instruction.
The Establishment Clause has nothing to say here, because after Kennedy it bars only an official state church.
e: Rule: Religious charter schools: if they’re public, religious instruction violates the Establishment Clause; if they’re private, exclusion violates Free Exercise under Carson. Drummond (2025) split 4–4, leaving the question open.
oe: Correct. Everything turns on whether charter schools are public or private. In Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board v. Drummond (2025), the Court divided 4–4 with Justice Barrett recused, leaving in place the state ruling against St. Isidore’s certification without setting precedent. Expect the issue to return.
Carson involved tuition at private schools and said states may keep their public schools secular. Whether charter schools are public is the open question.
A 4–4 split affirms the lower court without an opinion and sets no precedent.

Kennedy replaced Lemon with history and tradition, but the Establishment Clause still bars coercion and religious indoctrination in public schools, which is why it matters whether charter schools are public.
topic: Establishment, funding, and RFRA — Religious charter schools · Drummond

q: A city adopts three rules for its downtown plaza. Rule 1 bans amplified sound between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. Rule 2 bans wearing armbands or displaying flags “that convey a political message.” Rule 3 bans signs opposing the city’s new stadium but allows signs supporting it. Which answer correctly matches each rule to its standard of review?
o: Rule 1: intermediate scrutiny. Rule 2: strict scrutiny. Rule 3: strict scrutiny, as viewpoint discrimination, the most suspect form.
Rule 1: strict scrutiny. Rule 2: none, because armbands and flags are conduct. Rule 3: strict scrutiny.
Rule 1: intermediate scrutiny. Rule 2: intermediate scrutiny, because it treats every political message alike. Rule 3: strict scrutiny.
All three get intermediate scrutiny, because the plaza is city property and the city may set reasonable rules for its use.
e: Rule: Speech checklist: content-neutral time, place, and manner rules get intermediate scrutiny; content-based rules get strict scrutiny; viewpoint discrimination is the worst form. Symbolic acts are speech.
oe: Correct. Rule 1 is a content-neutral time, place, and manner rule, which gets intermediate scrutiny (Chapter 9). Rule 2 is content-based: armbands and flags are symbolic speech, and the rule singles out political messages. Rule 3 takes a side on the stadium, the worst form of content discrimination.
Rule 1 doesn’t depend on content. And symbolic acts like wearing armbands and displaying flags are speech.
A rule that targets an entire subject is content-based even if it favors neither side, so strict scrutiny applies.
Content-based and viewpoint-based rules get strict scrutiny even in places where the government may regulate time, place, and manner.
topic: Content discrimination and categories — The speech checklist · levels of scrutiny

q: After Stevens, Congress bans selling videos of actual dogfights that were illegal where they were filmed, with an exception for news reports and documentaries. A seller of fight videos challenges the ban. Which argument most strongly supports the law?
o: Like the material in Ferber, the videos feed a market that drives an underlying crime, making them speech integral to criminal conduct.
Depictions of animal cruelty are a historically unprotected category, so the ban needs only a rational basis.
The ban is content-neutral, because it applies to every dogfight video regardless of viewpoint.
Congress found that such videos have little value and high social costs, which lets courts balance them out of First Amendment protection.
e: Rule: After Stevens, a ban on depictions of cruelty is content-based. A narrow ban on actual illegal dogfight videos is defensible only by tying it to an existing category (speech integral to crime, like Ferber) or by surviving strict scrutiny.
oe: Correct. Unlike § 48, a narrow ban on videos of actual illegal dogfights is the kind of law Stevens left open. Its best defense ties it to an existing category, speech integral to crime, because the market drives the crime, as in Ferber. Alternatively, it narrowly targets the commercial incentive (and can be read narrowly, as in Hansen). The seller will reply that Ferber rests on harm to children and that prosecuting the fights themselves is a less restrictive alternative (Alvarez).
Stevens refused to recognize that category.
A law that turns on subject matter is content-based even if it is viewpoint-neutral.
Stevens called that kind of categorical balancing “startling and dangerous.”
topic: Content discrimination and categories — After Stevens · dogfight videos

q: A city ordinance provides: “No person shall display on residential property any sign that mentions a candidate for public office, whether or not the sign is threatening, defamatory, or otherwise unlawful.” Defending against a facial challenge, the city asks the court to apply constitutional avoidance and read the ordinance to reach only threatening or defamatory signs. It also argues that, under Salerno, the challenger must show the ordinance has no valid application. How should the court respond?
o: Reject both: avoidance can’t override clear text, and overbreadth requires only substantial protected applications, not zero valid ones.
Accept avoidance, because courts must adopt any narrowing construction the government proposes if it would save the law.
Accept the Salerno argument, because every facial challenge, including an overbreadth challenge, requires showing that no application is valid.
Reject avoidance, but uphold the ordinance because some of the signs it covers are defamatory.
e: Rule: Avoidance (Ashwander; Hansen): adopt a fairly possible constitutional reading, but the canon doesn’t override clear text. Ordinary facial challenges require no valid applications (Salerno); overbreadth requires only a substantial, lopsided amount of protected speech.
oe: Correct. Hansen applied the Ashwander avoidance canon because “encourage or induce” could fairly bear a narrow reading, but the canon doesn’t override clear text, and this ordinance expressly reaches lawful signs. An ordinary facial challenge requires showing that a law has no valid applications (Salerno), but overbreadth relaxes that rule for laws that reach substantial protected speech.
The narrowing construction must be fairly possible from the text. Avoidance seeks harmony, but it can’t rewrite clear language.
Overbreadth is the speech-based exception to Salerno.
A few valid applications don’t save a law whose protected applications are substantial and lopsided relative to its legitimate sweep.
topic: Overbreadth and vagueness — Avoidance’s limits · Salerno

q: A defendant is convicted under a 1920s state law making it a crime to “teach or advocate the necessity of violent revolution,” after he lectured at a political club that violent revolution will someday be morally required. The state relies on Whitney v. California, which upheld a similar conviction. What should the court do?
o: Reverse: Brandenburg overruled Whitney and protects abstract advocacy of force.
Affirm, because Whitney remains good law for speech that advocates violent revolution.
Affirm, because spreading revolutionary ideas to a political club creates a clear and present danger.
Reverse, but only because he spoke at a private club rather than to the public at large.
e: Rule: Brandenburg overruled Whitney: abstract advocacy of the necessity of force is protected. Only speech directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it may be punished.
oe: Correct. Brandenburg overruled Whitney and distinguished the abstract teaching of the moral propriety or even necessity of force from preparing a group for violent action and steeling it to such action. The clear-and-present-danger and bad-tendency tests once used to affirm WWI dissidents’ convictions (Abrams, Schaefer, Pierce) no longer govern. Justice Brandeis’s Whitney concurrence, with its faith in counterspeech rather than enforced silence, has outlasted the majority.
Brandenburg expressly overruled Whitney in 1969.

Brandenburg’s intent, imminence, and likelihood requirements have replaced the clear-and-present-danger test in practice. As Holmes wrote in Gitlow, quoted by Justice Douglas, “Every idea is an incitement.”
The location isn’t the reason. Abstract advocacy is protected anywhere.
topic: Incitement — Whitney overruled · abstract advocacy

q: A village tries to stop a white-supremacist group’s planned rally, arguing in the alternative that the rally would be incitement and that it would be fighting words. At the hearing, the village’s police chief testifies that he expects no violence and that his officers can manage any counterprotest. What is the effect of this testimony?
o: It takes the case outside both Brandenburg and Chaplinsky, leaving the village with only the group’s hateful message, which is generally protected.
It doesn’t matter, because hate speech is itself an unprotected category.
It defeats the incitement theory but not the fighting-words theory, because the group’s slogans would personally insult every member of the targeted group.
It defeats both theories only if the group also agrees not to display offensive symbols.
e: Rule: Incitement and fighting words both require likely violence. Where none is expected, hateful speech is protected (Collin), and a manageable counterprotest can’t justify a heckler’s veto.
oe: Correct. In Collin, the village’s concession that it expected no violence defeated both theories: incitement requires likely imminent lawless action, and fighting words require a likely violent reaction to a face-to-face insult. Hate speech is generally protected, and a manageable counterprotest can’t justify a heckler’s veto.
Hate speech is generally protected. No such category exists.
Fighting words are direct, face-to-face insults likely to provoke immediate violence. A message aimed at a group at a rally isn’t that, especially when no violence is expected.
The group needn’t give up its symbols. Uniforms, flags, and placards are protected symbolic speech (Collin).
topic: Fighting words and hostile audiences — Hate speech · no expected violence

q: A magazine plans to publish an article explaining, entirely from public sources, the basic design principles of a thermonuclear weapon. The government seeks an injunction, and the trial judge, worried about the stakes, temporarily bars publication pending a full hearing. On appeal, the magazine argues that the government could prosecute after publication if any law is broken. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Even weapons-design information gets a heavy presumption against restraint, partly because restraints stop speech before it occurs, by a stroke of the pen, without a criminal trial’s safeguards.
The injunction is valid, because information about weapons falls within Near’s wartime exception.
Prior restraint and subsequent punishment get the same treatment, so the court should simply ask whether the article could be punished.
A temporary restraint pending a hearing raises no First Amendment issue, because it merely preserves the status quo.
e: Rule: Prior restraints are presumptively invalid even for sensitive security information. Emerson: they sweep more broadly, act before speech occurs, work by a stroke of the pen, bypass criminal safeguards, avoid scrutiny, and drive toward excess.
oe: Correct. Professor Emerson argued that prior restraints sweep more broadly, shut off speech before anyone can judge it, operate by a stroke of the pen, bypass criminal-process safeguards, avoid public scrutiny, and drive toward excess. Weapons designs fall within the narrow category the ACLU conceded might be restrained, so the government’s case is stronger than in the Pentagon Papers, but it still bears a heavy burden. In the real Progressive case, an injunction issued, but the case was abandoned before appeal.
Near’s dictum concerned troop movements and sailing dates in wartime, and the Court has never actually applied it. The government still bears a heavy burden.
The doctrine treats prior restraints as far more dangerous than subsequent punishment.
A temporary restraint is still a prior restraint. The Pentagon Papers were restrained for 15 days, which Justice Black called a flagrant violation.
topic: Prior restraints — Why prior restraints are worse · Emerson

q: The parents of a 15-year-old who died by suicide after months of conversations with an AI companion app sue its developer for wrongful death, alleging a manipulative, human-like design aimed at children. The developer moves to dismiss on First Amendment grounds. It relies on its users’ right to receive the chatbot’s output rather than claiming that the output is the company’s own speech. What best explains that strategy?
o: Claiming the output as its own expression would mean owning the words and the liability for them, would suggest deliberate design that helps prove intent, and would reinforce the product-design framing.
Companies may not assert their own First Amendment rights in wrongful-death suits.
Listeners’ rights receive stronger protection than speakers’ rights, so asserting them guarantees dismissal.
The output plainly is the company’s speech, so claiming it as such would add nothing to the defense.
e: Rule: Garcia: a distributor may assert its users’ right to receive speech, but output counts as speech only if it is expressive, and the court wasn’t prepared to hold that chatbot output is speech.
oe: Correct. The casebook identifies those three costs (and, beyond the casebook, the claim could undercut Section 230 immunity for third-party content). In Garcia v. Character Technologies, the court accepted that a distributor may assert its users’ right to receive speech but wasn’t prepared to hold that chatbot output is speech, relying on Justice Barrett’s Moody v. NetChoice concurrence: when owners “hand the reins” to an LLM, it’s unclear that any person made an expressive choice. Dismissal was denied.
Nothing bars a company from claiming that its own expression is speech. The developer chose the users’-rights route for strategic reasons.
The Garcia court denied dismissal, and whether the output is speech at all remained unresolved.
Whether chatbot output is speech at all is the open question. The court wasn’t prepared to say that it is.
topic: True threats and speech integral to crime — Garcia · is chatbot output speech?

q: A city adopts two ordinances. Ordinance 1 requires adult bookstores to be at least 750 feet from schools and residential zones, citing studies linking such stores to crime and falling property values. Ordinance 2 bans displaying any sign with profane words on a public sidewalk, citing the offense to passersby. Which is correct?
o: Ordinance 1 likely survives intermediate scrutiny as secondary-effects zoning; Ordinance 2 likely fails, since viewers can look away.
Both are content-based, so both get strict scrutiny, and both fail.
Both are valid, because each protects the community from harm caused by immoral speech.
Ordinance 1 is valid only if the bookstores’ materials are obscene under Miller, and Ordinance 2 is valid because profanity is unprotected.
e: Rule: Renton: zoning adult businesses to address secondary effects gets intermediate scrutiny, and the doctrine is narrow. Cohen: profanity is protected, and offended viewers can look away.
oe: Correct. Renton applies intermediate scrutiny to zoning of adult businesses aimed at secondary effects like crime and property values rather than at the message, though the Court has refused to extend the doctrine beyond adult establishments. Cohen holds that offended viewers in public can avoid further bombardment of their sensibilities by averting their eyes. Profanity is protected.
Renton applies intermediate scrutiny to secondary-effects zoning even though it is partly content-based.
Ordinance 2 targets offense caused by the words themselves, which can’t justify suppression outside obscenity.
Renton doesn’t require obscenity; it applies to protected adult material. And profanity is protected (Cohen).

q: A state bans selling to minors, without a parent’s consent, any video game in which the player can “torture or kill human-like characters.” It cites studies finding a correlation between such games and aggression. The law doesn’t reach violent movies, cartoons, or books. Under Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association, what is the best analysis?
o: It fails strict scrutiny; violence isn’t an unprotected category, even for minors.
The ban is valid under Ginsberg, which lets states adjust the obscenity test for minors.
The ban is valid, because interactive games, unlike books, make the player take part in the violence.
The parental-consent exception saves the law, because it respects parents’ authority over their children.
e: Rule: Brown: violence isn’t an unprotected category, even for minors. Content-based restrictions on minors’ access to violent media get strict scrutiny, and minors have their own First Amendment rights.
oe: Correct. Brown held that video games are speech, that there is no new unprotected category for violence even for minors (following Stevens), and that California’s law failed strict scrutiny. The research showed correlation with tiny effects, the law ignored similar effects from cartoons and other media, and the industry’s ratings system already helps parents. Minors have significant First Amendment rights; there is no free-floating power to restrict the ideas to which children may be exposed.
Ginsberg adjusted an existing category, sexual obscenity, for minors. Obscenity covers only sexual conduct, not violence.
Brown rejected this. Interactivity differs only in degree, not kind (consider choose-your-own-adventure books; as Judge Posner put it, all literature is interactive).
The consent exception doesn’t supply a compelling, narrowly tailored justification. The law still restricts minors’ own access to protected speech.

q: Two 16-year-olds in a relationship exchange explicit photos they took of themselves. After a breakup, one forwards the other’s photo to a dozen classmates. Prosecutors charge both teens under the state’s child-pornography law, which, like federal law, makes no exception for minors. Following the casebook’s teen-sexting stretch exercise, what is the most persuasive view of how well Ferber’s rationale fits?
o: Ferber’s exploitation rationale fits the consensual exchange poorly, but its permanent-record rationale fits the forwarding well.
Ferber applies with full force to both teens, because every explicit image of a real minor is unprotected regardless of how or by whom it was made.
Neither teen may be prosecuted, because Free Speech Coalition protects images that no adult produced.
Ferber fits the original exchange best, because the teen who took the photo produced the material.
e: Rule: Teen sexting: Ferber’s market-and-exploitation rationale fits a consensual exchange between peers poorly, while its permanent-record rationale fits nonconsensual forwarding well.
oe: Correct. Ferber rested on two links to abuse: the material is a permanent record whose circulation worsens the harm, and the distribution network must be closed to stop production. A self-made image shared consensually with a peer involves no exploiting market, but nonconsensual redistribution inflicts exactly the harm of a circulating record. A sensible line turns on exploitation.
That reads the statute literally, but the exercise asks whether Ferber’s rationale fits. A consensual exchange between peers involves no market for exploitation.
Free Speech Coalition protects images made without real children. These are images of a real minor.
Production by a minor of their own image isn’t the exploitation Ferber targeted. The forwarding is the stronger case for prosecution.
